prerequisites: Basic notions of technical drawing (high school level 2) are recommended to facilitate understanding and proper follow-up.

learning_outcomes.text: Ability for spatial vision and knowledge of graphic representation techniques, both by traditional methods of metric and descriptive geometry, and by computer-aided design applications.

syllabus_topics: Topic 1. General concepts. Forms of communication in industry. Design and its evolution. Industry, Engineering and its languages. Basic drawing tools. Graphic expression and CAD in engineering. Computer-aided design: possibilities and most common systems.
Topic 2. Standardization in graphic expression. Standardization processes in industrial drawing. Standardization agencies. Common regulations for technical drawing in the industrial sector.

Topic 3. Geometric fundamentals of engineering design. Geometry applied to engineering design. Concepts, types and relationships. Metric Geometry. Geometric Constructions. Tangencies, homotheties and inversions.
Topic 4. Descriptive geometry, projections and representation systems. Description and uses. Representation and projection systems. The point, the line and the plane.

Topic 5. Dihedral representation system. Orthogonal representation. Concept of elevation, plan and profile. European and American systems. Correspondence between views. Common views and special views.

Topic 6. Axonometric, cavalier and conical perspectives. Axonometric system. Typical cases: isometric perspective vs. isometric drawing. Functionality and operability in industry. Advantages and disadvantages of its use. Cavalier perspective. Similarities and differences with respect to isometric perspective. Reduction coefficients. Conical perspective.

Topic 7. Representation of sections, cuts and breaks. Definition of the concepts cut, section and break. Common types of cuts and sections. Applicable standardization for the representation of cuts and sections.

Topic 8. Dimensioning. Basic concepts in dimensioning: parts of a dimension. Standardization for dimensioning elements. Common dimensioning systems. Dimensioning in orthogonal plane and isometric perspective.
Topic 9. General methodology for drawing plans. Formats, lines and scales. Coordinates. Plan handling: folding and storage.

Topic 10. Types of industrial plans and drawings. Most common types of drawings and plans. Assembly and exploded view drawings. Functionality in design and engineering. Examples of assemblies and exploded views in typical industrial equipment.

Topic 11. “Block diagrams, flow diagrams, process diagrams” Industrial processes. Diagrams for material and energy balances. Practical applications. Relationship between block diagrams and flow diagrams. Reference between them. Flow or process diagrams.

Topic 12. “Piping and instrumentation diagrams” Piping design and its standards. Types of piping plans. Instrumentation and its standards. Use in the design of piping and accessories. P&I's (Piping & Instruments) diagrams.

Topic 13. Computer-aided design (i): Introduction to CAD software. The CAD working environment: familiarization and customization. Basic commands for file management. Unit and coordinate systems. Drawing precision: data entry, entity selection and object snapping. Basic geometry: editing points, lines, polylines and simple geometric figures. Editing and modifying the drawing: intersections, trim/extend, fillet, chamfer, join/explode, copy/paste, symmetry and scaling. Magnification factors relative to original size and display. Screen redraw. Texts.

Topic 14. Computer-aided design (ii): advanced CAD software. Drawing hatching: patterns and uses. Dimensioning and its standards in CAD. Concept of layer: utility in industrial drawing. Creation, editing and deletion of layers. Creation and management of blocks. External references and their utility in teamwork.
assessment_rules: The general assessment model is continuous assessment. No single assessment activity may exceed 60% of the global grade, and non-re-evaluable activities may not exceed 40%. A minimum score of 4.5 out of 10 is required for the written theoretical-practical test and the AutoCAD practical test. To pass the course, the weighted average of all activities must be at least 5 out of 10, provided all minimum scores are met; otherwise, the final grade will be 4 out of 10. Students who fail or do not attend the ordinary call may only retake the re-evaluable activities in the extraordinary call. Computer lab practices and group work are not re-evaluable.
